title: The Hybrid Origin of Brāhmī Script from Aramaic, Phoenician and Greek Letters
ask_addressed: Open modern scholarship on the origin of Brahmi (Salomon 1998; Falk 2018; Indi@logs hybrid-origin paper)
quote: I argue that Brāhmī was not derived from a single script, but instead was a hybrid invention by Indian scholars from Aramaic, Phoenician and Greek letters
summary: Proposes Brahmi as a deliberate hybrid of Aramaic, Phoenician and Greek letters. Its introduction also states there is no consensus on Brahmi's origin and cites Salomon 1998 and Falk 1993/2018 (second-hand, not opened here).
limits: Single-author minority proposal by a non-specialist-institution author; letter-by-letter comparison argument, no new inscriptional evidence; Phoenician/Greek input and 'western Semitic trader' are inferred. Salomon and Falk claims here are only as reported by Pillai.

strand.from: Achaemenid Aramaic, Phoenician and Greek writing
strand.what: letterforms for Brahmi, with indigenous Indian scholars as inventors

title: Writing Systems: General Historical and Analytical / Writing Systems: Recent Script-Related Research (ch. 9, ed. E. Bashir)
venue: Chapter 9 'Writing systems' in a handbook on South Asian languages (volume title not shown on opened PDF)
ask_addressed: Open modern scholarship on the origin of Brahmi (Salomon 1998; Falk 2018; Indi@logs hybrid-origin paper)
quote: it remains possible, though by no means certain, that he or his immediate predecessors may have invented the Brahmi script on the model of Kharosthi
summary: Specialist overview: Kharosthi is tied to Achaemenid Aramaic scribal practice and dated no later than the 4th c. BCE; for Brahmi, there is no conclusive evidence for writing in mainland India before Asoka, so creation by Asoka or predecessors on the Kharosthi model is possible.
limits: Overview chapter, not a new analysis; cautious ('by no means certain'). Year not shown on the opened page. Brahmi-from-Kharosthi is one position among several (Falk-type creation view), not consensus.

strand.what: model for the Brahmi script, possibly invented under or just before Asoka

title: Ancient Egypt and the earliest known stages of alphabetic writing
venue: In Boyes & Steele (eds), Understanding Relations Between Scripts II: Early Alphabets, Oxbow, pp. 53-67
ask_addressed: the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions (Darnell et al. 2005), the Proto-Sinaitic decipherment debate
quote: the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions have largely remained undeciphered, the Wadi el-Ḥôl texts entirely so
summary: Egyptologist's review: Proto-Sinaitic and Wadi el-Hol datings are controversial (Hamilton c.1850-1700; Sass later c.1300 BC); Darnell's early-Middle-Kingdom reading is attractive but rests on two inscriptions of at most 28 signs; the Egyptian inspiration of the script remains obscure.
limits: Quote verified against the opened PDF (check_quote reached it only via a signed redirect URL). Sceptical stance on dating and decipherment, not a denial of Egyptian sign models.

title: Proto-Sinaitic – Progenitor of the Alphabet
ask_addressed: the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions (Darnell et al. 2005), the Proto-Sinaitic decipherment debate
quote: The proto-Sinaitic script almost certainly used the principle of acrophony to assign phonetic values to its signs.
summary: Argues Proto-Sinaitic is the first alphabet, drawing its signs from Egyptian hieroglyphic and hieratic and assigning values acrophonically; notes several scholars deny acrophony.
limits: Online journal article, 2011 (older than the 2019+ reviews); the author's own decipherment readings are contested; acrophony is denied by some.

title: Early alphabetic writing in the ancient Near East: the 'missing link' from Tel Lachish
authors: Höflmayer, F., Misgav, H., Webster, L., Streit, K.
ask_addressed: the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions (Darnell et al. 2005), the Proto-Sinaitic decipherment debate
quote: The date for the development of early alphabetic script is still disputed
summary: Reports a Lachish inscription argued to bridge the gap between Sinai/Egypt (19th-18th c. BC) and later Levantine alphabetic texts; also records that the dating of the earliest alphabet is disputed (Sass's lower dates vs Darnell's Wadi el-Hol dates).
limits: The quote is the article's own statement of the dispute; the Lachish reading is the authors' proposal and gap-filling is argued, not settled.

strand.what: alphabetic script spread and continuity across the Middle-to-Late Bronze Age

title: Digital Imaging and Archaeometric Analysis of the Cascajal Block: Establishing Context and Authenticity for the Earliest Known Olmec Text
authors: Englehardt, J.D., Insaurralde Caballero, M.A., Melgar Tísoc, E.R., Velázquez Maldonado, L.R., Guzmán Torres, V., Bernard, H.N., Carrasco, M.D.
ask_addressed: the dating of Chinese and Mesoamerican writing (Cascajal block, Rodriguez Martinez et al. 2006)
quote: Doubts linger, however, regarding the object’s authenticity,
summary: Re-examines the Cascajal block with imaging and pXRF; reports its material and manufacture are consistent with securely provenanced Olmec serpentine and argues this supports authenticity, while stating doubts persist (Bruhns et al. 2007; Cyphers 2007) over its lack of secure context.
limits: Authenticity is supported by material comparison, not by excavation context; the block remains undated by direct methods; whether its signs are true writing is a separate question.

title: The Cascajal Block: The Earliest Precolumbian Writing
ask_addressed: the dating of Chinese and Mesoamerican writing (Cascajal block, Rodriguez Martinez et al. 2006)
quote: Clearly associated with the Olmec civilization and dating to between approximately 1000 and 800 BCE, this script is the earliest in Mesoamerica
summary: Summarises Rodriguez Martinez et al., Science 313 (2006), the original claim: 62 signs on a serpentine block near San Lorenzo, dated about 1000-800 BCE by associated ceramics.
limits: Secondary summary of the Science paper (which was not opened); its date rests on associated ceramics in a quarry debris pile, a point later critics press. The Science article itself was a paywalled gap.
